sections.h2: Can a squatter become the owner of a Louisiana house?
sections.html:
Yes, but only after a long stretch of open possession. Louisiana calls it acquisitive prescription, and it takes ten years with good faith and just title, or thirty years without them.

Civil Code article 3473 allows ownership of immovables by ten years of prescription, and article 3475 lists the requisites: ten years of possession, good faith, just title, and a thing that can be acquired this way. Article 3486 allows thirty years of possession without just title or good faith. Someone who simply moves into an empty house usually has neither title nor good faith, so thirty years is the path for a true squatter.

RouteTimeNeedsArticle
Ten year prescription10 yearsGood faith and just titleC.C. 3473, 3475
Thirty year prescription30 yearsPossession onlyC.C. 3486

Article 3488 applies the ten year rules to thirty year prescription where they fit.

Possession has to be physical, visible and unbroken. Under article 3476 the possessor needs corporeal possession, or civil possession that was preceded by corporeal possession.

  • Continuous and uninterrupted.
  • Peaceable, so taking a house by force does not count.
  • Public and unequivocal, so hiding in a vacant house does not count either.

Article 3481 presumes good faith, and a mistake about facts or law does not defeat it. The presumption falls only if the possessor knew or should have known he was not the owner. Under article 3482, good faith matters at the start, and bad faith that develops later does not stop the ten year clock.

These attributes must hold for the entire period, which is why a gap in possession matters.

sections.h2: Just title and why it matters
sections.html:
Just title is a written transfer that would have moved ownership if the seller had really owned the property. It separates a ten year claim from a thirty year one.

Louisiana's transfer without warranty connects here. Article 2502 makes such a transfer a just title for prescription, with no presumption of bad faith. A person who buys rights from someone who did not actually own the house, then possesses it openly, can start the ten year clock. A squatter with no paper at all is stuck on the thirty year route.

If someone has lived on your land for many years, perhaps an unrecorded family member or a neighbor, get a lawyer's view before assuming your title is safe.

sections.h2: Removing an occupant who has no right to be there
sections.html:
The owner gives written notice to vacate and then goes to court by summary rule to show cause. Code of Civil Procedure article 4702 requires written notice once the purpose of the occupancy has ended, and gives the occupant five days from delivery to leave.

Article 4731 covers what comes next. If the occupant does not comply, the owner or agent may summarily cite the occupant to show cause why possession should not be delivered, and the citation must state the grounds. After the required notice, an owner who reasonably believes the premises are abandoned may take possession without more judicial process. The article lists signs such as stopped use, returned keys and removed belongings.

  • After a federal disaster declaration, stopping residential use is not treated as abandonment for 30 days.
  • A residential tenant locked out in violation of the article may recover the greater of $500 or twice the monthly rent.
  • The court may award costs and attorney fees to the winner.

Do not change locks or remove belongings without legal advice. Self help can cost the owner money.

R.S. 9:5633.1 lets a possessor acquire blighted property by three years of prescription, but only in certain municipalities, and in Lake Charles with city council approval. It is not a statewide rule.

The property must have been declared blighted after an administrative hearing, and the possessor must file an affidavit and the city's resolution in the mortgage and conveyance records. The owner and every mortgage holder receive certified mail within thirty days, and a notice goes on the building within a month.

  • The possessor must take peaceable possession and begin repairs within a reasonable time, not more than 45 days.
  • All ad valorem taxes, interest and penalties must be paid.
  • Owners of adjoining land have a first right to claim the property.
  • Recorded mortgages and liens are not wiped out.
  • The owner can bring a real action, and must then reimburse the possessor's costs and improvements.

An owner of a neglected house in Lake Charles or another covered city should deal with code citations before they turn into this kind of claim.

Houses left empty after a storm are the ones most often occupied without permission, and Louisiana has had plenty of storms. The eviction statute reflects this: under article 4731, in parishes covered by a federal disaster declaration, stopping residential use of a home is not treated as evidence of abandonment for 30 days after the declaration.

If you own a damaged house you cannot repair, keep records showing you still hold it, and consider a quick sale before an occupancy problem develops.

A cash sale skips the repair and financing hurdles that damaged houses run into, though the buyer will still want the occupancy question settled before closing. Put the sequence in order: confirm who holds the keys, serve the five day notice if someone is inside without a right to be there, and file the rule to show cause if they stay. Each step leaves a paper trail that a title company will ask to see.

sections.h2: Before selling a house someone else occupies
sections.html:
Find out who is there and on what basis, then clear the occupancy or disclose it before listing. Possession that has run for years can affect who owns the house.

Article 531 allocates the burden of proof. A person claiming ownership against someone who has possessed for ten years, or for one year in good faith with just title, must prove he acquired ownership from a previous owner or by prescription. In other cases he need only prove a better title. So the length of the occupant's stay decides who carries the burden.

  • Pull the deed and mortgage records from the parish clerk.
  • Write down when the occupant arrived and whether you ever consented.
  • Serve the written notice to vacate and keep proof of delivery.
  • Keep your own tax bills and receipts as evidence that you treat the house as yours.

faqs.q: How long does adverse possession take in Louisiana?
faqs.a: Ten years with good faith and just title, or thirty years without them, under Civil Code articles 3473, 3475 and 3486. The possession must also be continuous, peaceable, public and unequivocal.

faqs.q: Do squatters have rights in Louisiana?
faqs.a: Not by moving in. A squatter usually has no title or good faith, so thirty years of possession would be needed. Until then the owner can remove the occupant through a written notice and a rule to show cause.

faqs.q: How much notice must an owner give a non-tenant occupant?
faqs.a: Five days, in writing, once the purpose of the occupancy has ended, under Code of Civil Procedure article 4702. If the person does not leave, the owner may seek a rule to show cause under article 4731.

faqs.q: Does paying property tax stop a squatter from taking my land?
faqs.a: Tax payment is not an element of the possession rules either way. What counts is possession that is uninterrupted, so an owner who sees someone on the land should act early and get legal advice.

faqs.q: Is there a three year adverse possession rule in Louisiana?
faqs.a: Only in narrow cases. R.S. 9:5633.1 allows it for blighted property in certain municipalities and in Lake Charles, with strict notices, repairs and tax payments. Ordinary property follows the ten and thirty year rules.
